segments.text: Statehood determines whether an entity qualifies as a state in international law; recognition concerns how other states respond to that status or to a government.
Study the classic statehood criteria, legal personality, declaratory and constitutive theories of recognition, de facto/de jure recognition, and the practical legal effects of recognition.

Statehood concerns whether an entity possesses the legal characteristics of a state. The frequently cited Montevideo formulation identifies a permanent population, defined territory, government and capacity to enter relations with other states. These criteria are useful, but modern disputes can also involve self-determination, unlawful territorial acquisition, effectiveness, external control and institutional recognition.

A defined territory does not require perfectly settled boundaries. Likewise, a government need not be free from every internal challenge. The deeper question is whether there is a sufficiently stable territorial-political community capable of operating as a state under international law.

The declaratory theory treats recognition as acknowledgement of a status that exists when the legal criteria for statehood are satisfied. The constitutive theory assigns recognition a stronger role in creating international legal status or the capacity to participate fully in the international community.

Modern practice often reflects elements of both approaches. An entity may claim statehood independently of recognition, yet widespread recognition can have major practical consequences for diplomatic relations, treaty participation, access to institutions, immunities and treatment in domestic courts.

Recognition of a state concerns the international legal personality of the territorial political entity. Recognition of a government concerns which authority is accepted as entitled to represent that state. Governments can change while the state remains the same legal person.

Contested examples should be used carefully. The learner should identify the legal question being illustrated—statehood, representation, self-determination or diplomatic recognition—without treating politically disputed claims as uncontested facts.

items.text: Statehood asks whether an entity possesses the legal characteristics of a state. Recognition asks how other states acknowledge and deal with that claimed status or with a government exercising authority.

The classic criteria focus on population, territory, government and capacity for international relations. In practice, statehood disputes can also involve self-determination, effectiveness and competing legal claims.
The declaratory view treats recognition mainly as acknowledgement of an existing legal fact; the constitutive view gives recognition a larger role in creating international legal status.
Recognition of a state and recognition of a government are distinct. A state may continue to exist even while other states dispute which authority should be treated as its government.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not say that recognition automatically creates statehood in every theory. Explain the competing theories and practical legal effects.

items.text: Learn statehood criteria and recognition theories separately.
Use contested-state examples carefully and neutrally.
Explain the difference between recognizing a state and recognizing a government.

segments.text: Statehood and recognition are related but not identical.
Recognition may have diplomatic and domestic legal consequences.
International organizations and individuals can possess forms of international legal personality too.
